steps.title: Prompt: Define the First Hour
steps.description: Use when: starting friction is the main problem. Provide: the foreground output and available tools. “Turn this output into the smallest first-hour sequence. Give me the first physical action, a 25-minute work block, and the exact evidence I should report when complete.”
steps.source_heading: Step 2: Prompt: Define the First Hour

steps.title: Prompt: Run the Arbitration Engine
steps.description: Use when: several options feel equally urgent. Provide: options, deadlines, upside, downside, and dependencies. “Compare these options using leverage, real urgency, compounding value, reversibility, and downside. Rank them, name the decision, and state what evidence would change the ranking.”
steps.source_heading: Step 3: Prompt: Run the Arbitration Engine

steps.title: Prompt: Separate Decision From Anxiety
steps.description: Use when: emotional pressure is making every option feel dangerous. “Separate the observable facts, assumptions, emotional predictions, and reversible experiments in this decision. Do not reassure me; show me the smallest test that produces new evidence.”
steps.source_heading: Step 4: Prompt: Separate Decision From Anxiety

steps.title: Prompt: Review Evidence, Not Intentions
steps.description: Use when: closing the week. Provide: completed, partial, and missed outputs. “Review this week by evidence. Identify what produced completed work, what repeatedly failed, and one operating rule to keep, change, or remove next week.”
steps.source_heading: Step 5: Prompt: Review Evidence, Not Intentions

steps.title: Prompt: Detect a Repeating Pattern
steps.description: Use when: the same commitment keeps slipping. “Compare these daily logs. Identify the repeated trigger, the behavior that follows, and the system change most likely to interrupt the pattern. Do not diagnose me.”
steps.source_heading: Step 6: Prompt: Detect a Repeating Pattern

steps.title: Prompt: Activate a Minimum Viable Day
steps.description: Use when: capacity is low but continuity matters. “Reduce today to one meaningful action, one basic maintenance floor, and a clean shutdown. Remove catch-up work and define what counts as enough.”
steps.source_heading: Step 7: Prompt: Activate a Minimum Viable Day

steps.title: Prompt: Match Task to Capacity
steps.description: Use when: the planned task exceeds current attention or energy. “Classify these tasks by cognitive load and consequence. Choose the highest-value task that fits my current capacity, then shrink it to a finishable block.”
steps.source_heading: Step 8: Prompt: Match Task to Capacity

steps.title: Prompt: Choose the One Winning Move
steps.description: Use when: the list is larger than the day. “From this list, choose the one action that creates the most leverage or removes the largest future bottleneck. Explain the choice in three criteria and park the rest.”
steps.source_heading: Step 9: Prompt: Choose the One Winning Move

steps.title: Prompt: Cut False Urgency
steps.description: Use when: every request arrives labeled urgent. “Sort these items into real deadline, consequence of delay, dependency, and perceived pressure. Return only the items that create a real cost if not handled today.”

steps.title: Short Answer
steps.description: This page fills the daily citation velocity gap for daily planning with a bounded ChatGPT workflow: name the situation, set one constraint, choose one executable next action, and close the loop with evidence. The purpose is not to create another elaborate productivity ritual. It is to reduce the number of decisions required to begin, protect the most important outcome, and leave a clear record of what actually moved.

steps.title: How to run the workflow
steps.description: Start with a plain description of the daily planning situation. Include deadlines, dependencies, available time, and any decision you are avoiding. Ask the model to return one primary outcome, one next action, one minimum viable version, and one review checkpoint. Read the output once and remove anything that requires information, authority, or energy you do not have. Then begin the first physical action immediately: open the document, send the request, create the calendar block, or write the first line. Keep the model in a constrained operating role. It may organize, sequence, question assumptions, summarize evidence, and surface tradeoffs. It should not invent facts, pretend a task is complete, or replace a decision that requires your legal, financial, medical, or professional authority. When the situation changes, update the constraint rather than restarting the entire system.
steps.source_heading: Step 2: How to run the workflow

steps.title: Common failure modes
steps.description: The first failure mode is asking for broad advice and receiving a broad answer. Replace “help me be better at daily planning” with the current state, constraint, and required decision. The second failure mode is accepting a plan with too many priorities. Force the response back to one outcome and one first action. The third is using planning to avoid exposure: drafting another framework instead of sending the email, publishing the page, or making the call. The fourth is treating a low-energy day as proof that the system failed. Use the minimum viable version and preserve continuity.

steps.title: Prompt
steps.description: Act as my Spry Executive OS chief of staff for daily planning. Use only the facts I provide. Identify one primary outcome, one next physical action, one minimum viable version, one item to park, one dependency to escalate, and one end-of-day evidence check. Respect my stated time and energy constraints. Do not give me a motivational list, invent progress, or add catch-up work.

steps.title: Example operating response
steps.description: A strong response is brief enough to use. Follow this response shape: That output converts daily planning from a vague concern into a sequence with ownership, boundaries, and proof. Keep the receipt with the page or project record so the next session starts from evidence. Reuse the same sequence for seven days before changing it. Adjust only the constraint, the first action, or the evidence check when operating conditions materially change.
